listenings.text: I've been studying older language learners for about fifteen years now, and the thing that surprised me most was how well they retain new words, as long as they use them in real conversation. In one of our studies, a group of learners over sixty-five did just as well as a group of university students after six months. The difference was that the older group needed more repetition, and they needed more time to feel confident. But they were far more consistent. They hardly ever missed a class. So when people ask me if it's too late, I always say: it's never too late. It's just a slightly different road.

I'm sixty-seven, and I've been learning Spanish for two years. Why Spanish? My daughter married a man from Seville, and at the wedding I could not say one word to his parents. I felt terrible. So the week after I came home, I found a teacher. I've had a class every Tuesday since then, and I've never missed one. Is it easy? No. My pronunciation is still very Indian, and I forget words all the time. But last month I reached a milestone. I had a whole conversation with my son-in-law's parents, on the phone, for twenty minutes. My wife says I have been smiling ever since.

Almost every learner I've worked with has hit a plateau at some point. It usually happens at the intermediate level. You've been studying for a few years, you can get by, and suddenly it feels like nothing is improving. Why? Because you keep doing the same things that worked at the beginning: the same textbook, the same kind of class. My advice is twofold. First, change the input. If you've been reading textbooks, start reading real books. If you've been listening to slow audio, switch to podcasts and series at full speed. Second, set a new goal, a concrete one. Not get better, but understand a whole film without subtitles by June. Plateaus don't last forever. Unless you stop.

reading.rtitle: Too Old to Learn? What Research Says
paras: For a long time, it was common to hear that languages are for children. After a certain age, people said, the brain simply stops learning. Researchers have been studying this question for decades, and today most of them agree that it is a myth, or at least a big exaggeration. Children do have an advantage with pronunciation: they pick up a native accent more easily. But in many other areas, adults learn faster, especially at the beginning.

Older learners bring real strengths. They have a larger vocabulary in their own language, they understand how grammar works, and they know how to study. Studies have shown that they retain new words well when they use them in real situations, instead of trying to memorize lists. What they often need is more time and more repetition. Above all, they need consistency: thirty minutes every day is worth more than four hours once a week.

Almost every adult learner reaches a plateau, usually at the intermediate level, when progress seems to stop. The ones who keep at it tend to change something: more exposure to real English, new materials, or a new goal. And there is a bonus. Some studies suggest that learning a language is excellent cognitive exercise and may help the brain stay active for longer. For many experts, the most important factor is not age but mindset.
